proof_coverage.topic: Exact theorem scope, definitions, and endpoints
checks: The problem is scalar: u is real-valued and Du is in R^n, n>=2. The growth exponents satisfy 1<p<=q<infinity; the coefficient exponent satisfies 0<alpha<=1. Vectorial regularity and p=1 are not claimed.

Theorem 1 is first a theorem about local minimizers of the LSM relaxation, not every finite-energy weak solution. Corollary 1 transfers it to minimizers of F only when the Lavrentiev gap vanishes on every compactly contained ball. Equation (1.16) verifies the required implication using F<=Fbar.

The gap q/p<1+alpha/n is strict. Page 48 explicitly excludes equality. The nondegenerate optimal Schauder conclusion requires mu>0, a uniform continuity modulus of D_zzF on bounded gradient sets, and alpha<1. No endpoint C^{1,1} assertion follows when the coefficients are Lipschitz.
For mu=0, the conclusion is a positive exponent alpha_* which may depend on the local energy and data. The theorem does not identify alpha_* with alpha.

Theorem 2 assumes u locally bounded and p<=n, and uses q<p+alpha min{1,p/2}. Its conclusion is every finite gradient-integrability exponent, not a uniform estimate at exponent infinity. Its sharpness assertion is expressly limited to p>=2.

The case q=p has zero gap and is included. The branch definitions match at p=2 and p=n. The main gap implies (7.9): for p<2, p alpha/n<=p alpha/2; for 2<=p<=n, p alpha/n<=alpha; for p>n it is exactly the third branch.
proof_coverage.outcome: No scope or endpoint contradiction found. The strictness and additional hypotheses must be preserved in the report.

proof_coverage.topic: Basic calculus, difference quotients, and relaxation
checks: The V_mu estimates have the expected p-growth scaling; E_mu=(H_mu^{p/2}-mu^p)/p is obtained by integrating t(t^2+mu^2)^{(p-2)/2}. Inequality (2.10) follows from the mean-value bound for E_mu combined with the V_mu metric equivalence. The p<2 alternative in (2.7) is required and is retained in later comparisons.

Lemma 2.1 is integration by parts for the finite difference of the bounded composite K(x,V(x)). The zero trace of W removes the boundary contribution. Mollification and dominated convergence are legitimate on the strictly larger ball; a bound on |z|<=||V||_infty+1 can be used for the mollified vector field. No differentiability of V is needed in the final statement.

The normalization F-F(x,0)+L(mu^q+mu^p) adds only an x-dependent energy term. It preserves minimizers and changes relaxed energies by the same fixed integral. The new integrand is still bounded below by the old one and gains (2.13) by integrating D_zF along the segment from 0 to z.

The domains and exponents in Lemmas 3.1-3.4 were tracked. For Lemma 3.4 the cut-off equals one on B_{(2theta+1)/3}, while |h|<(1-theta)/4 keeps x and x+h in that region for x in B_theta. Rescaling gives the stated rho^{-s} and average-volume factors.
The local second-difference result, Lemma 3.2, is applied only with 1<s<2 and m>1. The proof later establishes both strict inequalities; it does not try to use the unavailable endpoint s=1.

Lemma 4.1 follows directly from Holder: the radial integrand is bounded by C ||f||_m^vartheta rho^{sigma-n*vartheta/m-1}, integrable exactly when m>n*vartheta/sigma. In the later application n/2>alpha*k, and the chosen gradient exponent is twice the threshold.

For Lemma 6.1, the recovery sequence follows by diagonal selection on weakly bounded energy sublevels; coercivity and compact embedding give strong L^p convergence. Convexity implies F<=Fbar, and a constant recovery sequence proves equality on W^{1,q}. Strict convexity in gradients is compatible with passage to relaxation via the quantitative p-ellipticity defect, not merely pointwise strict convexity.

In Lemma 6.2, truncation above the strictly enlarged L-infinity bound affects a set whose measure tends to zero. D wbar_j=D w_j times its complement indicator; pairing with a fixed L^{p'} vector field justifies weak-gradient convergence. Replacing gradients by zero costs at most 2L mu^p times the shrinking measure. This proves bounded recovery without an unproved maximum principle.
proof_coverage.outcome: Internal uses are consistent. Several general embedding and relaxation inputs are cited from the literature; their full original proofs were not all independently inspected.

checks: The proposition assumes an already Lipschitz, C^{1,beta} solution, beta in (0,alpha), mu>0, alpha<1, and uniform-in-x continuity of D_zA on bounded gradient sets. It is not used as an unconditional substitute for the main Lipschitz theorem.

In the p<2 extension, the frozen operator includes r^alpha H_mu^{(q-2)/2} z, ensuring the Dirichlet comparison is defined in W^{1,q}. Monotonicity and the coefficient difference lead to (5.9). Young's exponents produce r^{alpha*p/(p-1)}, which is at most r^{2alpha} for r<=1 because p/(p-1)>2.

The V_mu comparison bound gives a uniform p-energy bound on v. The imported autonomous estimate (5.7), whose denominator (n+1)p-nq is positive under (5.3), then bounds Dv on the half-ball. The p<2 metric equivalence yields the unweighted L^2 comparison on the half-ball, proving the printed (5.6).

After the comparison gradient is bounded, the linearized matrix is uniformly elliptic with constants allowed to depend on mu and the bound H. De Giorgi-Nash-Moser plus the stated derivative modulus provides the continuous-coefficient linear theory used in the final Campanato step.

To apply the proposition after (1.18), choose beta<min{alpha,alpha_*}; a C^{0,alpha_*} gradient on the larger ball is also C^{0,beta}. Thus the strict beta<alpha requirement is met even if alpha_*>=alpha.
The p>=2 argument and the final Campanato transfer are explicitly imported from [26]. Their use and needed hypotheses were tracked, but a new full proof of those external parts is not claimed.
proof_coverage.outcome: The new p<2 comparison is algebraically consistent; the conclusion remains conditional on the identified external regularity inputs.

proof_coverage.topic: Higher integrability: test equation and three p-regimes
checks: Proposition 7.2 is an a priori statement for smooth regularized integrands with positive mu and a q-coercivity coefficient L_star^{-1}. Initial local C^1 regularity permits all finite powers and the test function. The estimates must, and do, remove dependence on L_star and mu; those parameters are only needed for initial admissibility and finiteness.

Fix kappa>0 with 2 kappa<min{p+gamma-q,alpha}; define g=p+gamma-q-kappa>0. With sigma=t-2q+p+1+2gamma-2kappa, the target exponent is m=sigma-1+p=t+2g. The critical cancellation sigma-1-2gamma+2kappa=1+vartheta*sigma-alpha-lambda=t-2q+p makes the (I) estimate in (7.31) an ordinary first-difference L^t bound.

The cut-off radii have gaps at least (tau2-tau1)/(24K), while |h|<(tau2-tau1)/(10^4 K). Thus shifts, double shifts, and the seven h_0 margin in Lemma 3.2 stay inside the domains. The test function eta^d |tau_h u|^{sigma-1} tau_h u has compact support and is admissible; d=max{p,2} prevents negative cut-off powers in the differentiated estimates.

For p>=2, the p-ellipticity defect controls |tau_h Du|^p. The positive definite averaged Hessian permits Cauchy-Schwarz for (IV); its Young term is absorbed in (III). For q=2 the Holder step with exponent q-2=0 is correctly omitted. The lower bound on the derivative of |tau_h u|^{(sigma-1)/p} tau_h u and the scalar power monotonicity produce the second-difference term (7.39).

For 2<=p<=n, gamma=alpha and lambda=kappa_0=0. The three fractional orders are strictly between zero and one: their denominator-minus-numerator margins are 1+alpha-2kappa, 2-2kappa, and p-2kappa. The Holder-integrability exponents do not exceed t because alpha<=1 and q>=p. Thus Lemma 3.4 is applied within its range in (7.42)-(7.44).

For p>n, delta1=p(alpha+1)/n-2kappa, delta2=2p/n-2kappa, delta3=p^2/n-2kappa lie in (0,sigma). All three displayed quotients in (7.47) equal exactly one; this was symbolically checked. The remaining integration powers are at most t: the relevant excesses contain p(alpha-1)/n, 2p(alpha-1)/n+(p-q), and 2(p-q)+p(2alpha-p)/n, respectively, all non-positive. First-difference estimates therefore apply directly.

For 1<p<2, a direct upper bound of the Hessian term would introduce singular factors. The manuscript instead combines (II)+(IV) and uses Lemma 2.1 on the whole flux. This is a substantive correct distinction. Young's conjugate exponents (2q-p)/(2-p) and (2q-p)/(2(q-1)) are positive and sum reciprocally to one.

In that subquadratic case, theta=t-2q+p(1+alpha). The three orders in (7.60) are in (0,1); in particular m-theta=p-2kappa>0 and the other two denominator margins are 2-(2-p)alpha-2kappa>p-1>0. Their corresponding gradient powers are <=t by alpha<=1 and q>=p. This checks the interpolation in (7.61).

After unification, beta0-1=2kappa/m for p<=n and beta0-1=2kappa*n/(p*m) for p>n. These are strictly positive and less than one because t>=t_*. Consequently Lemma 3.2 applies, and beta0 tends to one only as the integration exponent tends to infinity; no forbidden endpoint application occurs.

The iteration t_i=t_*+2ig increases linearly. For each prescribed finite target exponent only finitely many steps are used. Interpolation with L^p then has power (t_*-p)/(t_{i+1}-p)<1, enabling Young absorption and the radius iteration. This removes the initial high-integrability norm without assuming a uniform bound as i tends to infinity.

To deduce Proposition 7.1, p>n uses Sobolev-Morrey and p<=n uses the external local-boundedness estimate [51]. Remark 7.1 explains why the doubling hypothesis there can be replaced by the currently available W^{1,q} regularity; the tail integral of F(x,2Du) tends to zero under q-growth. The full [51] proof was not separately read.
The main gap implies the chosen non-dimensional branch bounds. For Theorem 2, local boundedness is an assumption, so Proposition 7.3 uses (1.26) directly without the stronger dimensional gap.
proof_coverage.outcome: The internal numerology and the finite-iteration logic were verified in all three p-regimes. External inputs and constants are separately qualified.

proof_coverage.topic: Approximation App(B), weak limits, and recovery of the intended minimizer
checks: The x-normalization from Section 2.3 is imposed before smoothing, so joint continuity and the x-mollification error are available. The x-mollifier stays inside Omega because delta<=dist(B,boundary Omega)/2.

The regularization F_epsilon,delta=F_delta+sigma_epsilon H_{mu+delta}^{q/2} has positive mu_delta and q-coercivity. The structural upper constant L_tilde is uniform in both parameters, while L_star is comparable to sigma_epsilon^{-1}; a priori results explicitly avoid that latter dependence.

Writing X=||D u_tilde_epsilon||_q^q gives sigma_epsilon X=X/(1+epsilon^{-1}+X^2)<=sqrt(epsilon)/2 and sigma_epsilon<=epsilon. This proves the vanishing artificial q-energy in (8.6), even if X diverges along the recovery sequence.

The mollification error is bounded by C delta^alpha(1+|z|)^q. For fixed epsilon, q-coercivity bounds the minimizing gradients in L^q and hence makes this error vanish as delta tends to zero. It is not uniform in epsilon; the paper correctly fixes epsilon first and then sends delta to zero.

The trace condition u_epsilon,delta-u_tilde_epsilon in W_0^{1,q} is retained under the fixed-epsilon weak limit. Poincare and the recovery sequence then give a bounded W^{1,p} sequence whose next limit u_bar lies in u+W_0^{1,p}.

Convex lower semicontinuity and the approximation-energy upper bound yield Fbar(u_bar,B)<=Fbar(u,B). Relaxed minimality gives the reverse inequality. The strict gradient convexity of Fbar and the zero boundary difference imply u_bar=u; thus the limiting estimates apply to the assigned minimizer, not merely to an unspecified selected solution.

The printed sentence that the sequence of gradients is bounded in W^{1,q} should be read as the sequence of functions being bounded in W^{1,q}; the displayed energy only bounds gradients in L^q, and that is exactly what the subsequent weak convergence uses. This harmless local wording is not an independent substantive concern.

For Theorem 2 the corrected weaker maximum estimate in Finding P1 is sufficient to control the regularized solutions. Applying the interior estimates first on B_{sigma rho} and then taking sigma up to one, as Remark 8.1 states, avoids an unjustified assumption of boundary C^1 regularity.

Every finite target gradient norm passes through delta then epsilon by weak lower semicontinuity. The L-infinity bound is obtained either weak-* locally or, as footnote 2 explicitly does, by taking each finite L^r average bound and then r to infinity. No exchange of the nonuniform regularization limits is needed.
proof_coverage.outcome: The order of limits and identification of the limiting minimizer are justified. The local correction to Lemma 8.1 preserves this chain.

proof_coverage.topic: Autonomous estimates, fractional Caccioppoli inequality, and higher-power remainder
checks: The main gap implies q/p<1+2/(n-1), so the imported autonomous estimates of Section 9 are available in their stated range. The comparison problem has Lipschitz boundary data and q-coercivity, making existence, uniqueness, and testing by u-v legitimate.

For n=2 or n>=4 the exponent s=2q/((n+1)p-(n-1)q) has a positive denominator. In n=3, q>p requires an exponent strictly larger than q/(2p-q); the proof later retains a positive margin rather than silently taking equality. For q=p, s=1.

The autonomous bound gives ||Dv||_infty<=C M^s on the half-ball, which changes the Caccioppoli coefficient from the ellipticity-ratio bound Mcal^{q-p} to C M^{s(q-p)}. This is the particular exponent needed later, not merely an unspecified Lipschitz estimate.

The two comparison equations cancel their common test u-v. For p>=2, the weighted Young inequality bounds the V_mu defect by rho^{2alpha}|h|^{2alpha beta0} integral H^{(2q-p)/2}. For p<2, the alternative V_mu inequality gives a second power p(q-1)/(2(p-1)); its difference from (2q-p)/2 is (2-p)(q-p)/(2(p-1))>=0. Also p/(p-1)>2 permits the same rho and h powers. These facts justify (10.13) for the full range p>1.

The passage from V_mu to E_mu uses the one-Lipschitz truncation and (2.10). Splitting V_mu^2 into powers 1-k and k makes the comparison remainder depend on a large finite gradient moment rather than on an extra large power of the unknown Lipschitz bound.

The parameter m=2+2b_k+ns/(2delta) exceeds 2b_k, q, and ns/(2delta). This makes the refinement ||Dv||_infty<=C|h|^{-2 beta0 delta}||Du||_m^s+C valid. All three remainders in (10.15) are dominated by the stated power 2 beta0(alpha k-p delta), because rho,|h|<=1 and 0<delta<alpha k/p.

Choosing beta0=1/(1+alpha k-p delta) exactly balances the difference-quotient power 1-beta0 with the comparison power beta0(alpha k-p delta). Thus alpha_tilde=(alpha k-p delta)/(1+alpha k-p delta) is positive and less than 1/2.

The cube lattice has uniformly bounded overlap after eightfold ball dilation and covers the half-ball up to a null set. The sum in (10.21) therefore has a constant independent of h; no loss proportional to the number of small balls is introduced.

In the product bound on page 42, use b_k<m/2, Holder for ||Du||_m^{ps}, and then Holder for integral H^{m/2}; their exponents ps/(m+ps) and m/(m+ps) add to one. This yields the single integral H^{(m+ps)/2}. The large remainder power is finite once k and delta have been fixed.

Lemma 3.1 is applied with beta strictly below alpha_tilde. The factor (alpha_tilde-beta)^{-1/2} is retained; the proof does not take the divergent endpoint. Fractional Sobolev gives chi=n/(n-2beta)>1, since n>=2 and beta<1/2.
proof_coverage.outcome: The internal comparison, covering, and exponent balances in Lemma 10.1 were verified. The autonomous estimate and original Caccioppoli statement remain identified external inputs.

proof_coverage.topic: Sharp-gap absorption, n=3 margin, and final Schauder transfer
checks: For alpha<1, alpha/(1+alpha)>alpha/2. Hence k close to one and delta close to zero can be chosen first so that alpha_tilde>alpha/2; then choose beta in (alpha/2,alpha_tilde). These choices are made before fixing the large finite remainder powers.
In Lemma 4.2, M0=Mstar=M^{s(q-p)/2}. Both output terms carry M^{s(q-p)chi/(2(chi-1))}=M^{tp}, where t=sn(q/p-1)/(4beta). Taking the pth root yields the same M^t in both terms of (10.29).

For the potential remainder, sigma=alpha k, vartheta=1/2, and n/2>alpha k. The selected target gradient exponent r=n*pbar/(alpha k) is strictly greater than n*pbar/(2alpha k), so Lemma 4.1 is used away from its forbidden endpoint.

Writing R=q/p and D=n+1-(n-1)R gives t=(R/D)*(n(R-1)/(2beta)) in dimensions 2 and at least 4. The first factor is <1 because D-R=1-n(R-1)>0. The second is <alpha/(2beta)<1 by the strict main gap. This establishes t<1 analytically.

For n=3, replace R/(4-2R) by R/(4-2R)+epsilon. Since R<1+alpha/3<=4/3 and the inequality is strict, one can choose epsilon>0 with this factor still <1. The strict increase in the autonomous exponent is therefore fully accommodated.

When q=p, t=0 and no Young absorption is required. When alpha=1, choose alpha' in (n(R-1),1); the local Lipschitz coefficient bound implies the alpha'-Holder bound on balls of diameter at most 4, with an allowed enlarged structural constant. This proves the Lipschitz and degenerate Schauder conclusions, not an endpoint C^{1,1} conclusion.

Young's inequality with t<1 and the radius iteration yield (10.41). Proposition 7.1 then controls the finitely many large gradient powers by the original L^p energy. Constants can diverge as the strict gap closes; no uniform borderline assertion is made.

After the ordered approximation limits, bounded Du makes D_zF(x,Du) bounded locally. The Euler equation initially obtained for smooth tests extends to all W_0^{1,1} tests by norm density. Convexity then proves F-minimality for every competitor in Definition 1, including those not initially known to belong to W^{1,q}.

For (1.18), monotonicity of A->Fbar(u,A) follows by restricting recovery sequences, so the uniform energy bound on the larger ball controls every smaller comparison ball. The paper imports the Campanato decay from [26] after supplying its required uniform Lipschitz bound; it explicitly explains that only q/p<1+2/n is needed at that stage, which follows here.

The final optimal exponent uses Proposition 5.1 on a strictly larger interior ball and beta<min{alpha,alpha_*}. The dependence on mu and the derivative modulus is retained. The fixed-ball covering then supplies the stated local Holder estimate.
proof_coverage.outcome: No confirmed invalid absorption or limiting step was found in this chain. The external [26] Campanato argument was not independently reconstructed in full.

checks: The paper contains no new explicit counterexample construction for the optimal gap. It cites [32] and [34], with further fractal examples [2] and [3], and summarizes the double-phase mechanism in Remark 10.3. Therefore the present review can track the stated hypotheses and implications, but cannot claim to have independently verified every detail of those external constructions.

The quoted counterexample range p<n<n+alpha<q indeed implies q/p>1+alpha/n. Taking p up to n from below and q down to n+alpha from above approaches the claimed ratio threshold. This supports optimality of the universal gap rate; it is not a proof of failure for every single fixed (p,q) above the threshold.

For bounded minimizers with p>=2, that same limiting range approaches q=p+alpha and is consistent with the asserted optimal non-dimensional gap. The paper does not claim that the subquadratic p alpha/2 threshold is proved optimal.

The double-phase Hessian has radial and tangential eigenvalues whose ratio is bounded in terms of p and q; this is consistent with the paper's distinction between bounded pointwise ellipticity ratio for that special structure and the more general setting.

At equality q/p=1+alpha/n, the double-phase special case can have additional structure-based regularity, while Theorem 1 leaves the general endpoint open. Page 48 states this explicitly. Missing the endpoint is not itself a defect in the strict theorem.

Non-vanishing Lavrentiev gaps distinguish minimizers of the original and relaxed functionals. The cited discontinuous original minimizers cannot automatically be used as counterexamples to Theorem 1 without checking relaxed minimality; this review does not make that invalid inference.
